analysis.one_liner: Sunsets most cable rate regulation while requiring cheap basic cable tiers and banning exclusive programming contracts.
analysis.headline: The bill — introduced jointly by a Republican and a Democrat with 4 cosponsors — never received any vote, sitting in a House subcommittee from August 1998 until the Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have ended FCC rate regulation of most cable TV packages after March 31, 1999, unless a local franchising authority certified the operator was failing to offer viewers a reasonable range of programming choices. In exchange, it would have required every cable operator to sell a cheap "lifeline" tier of local channels at FCC-regulated reasonable rates, and extended rules barring exclusive contracts for satellite-delivered programming so competitors like satellite TV could carry the same networks as cable. It died in a House subcommittee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, cable subscribers would have gained the right to buy a bare-bones, price-regulated local-channels tier instead of being forced into expensive packages. Satellite TV providers and their subscribers would have gained from the ban on exclusive distribution contracts, which would let satellite services carry popular networks that cable-affiliated companies controlled. Cable operators themselves would also have benefited, because rate regulation of their expanded programming tiers would largely end.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Cable subscribers, satellite TV competitors, and cable operators

how_it_helps.text: Requires every cable operator to offer a separately packaged 'lifeline' tier made up only of local broadcast signals, public/educational/government access channels, and other locally carried stations, with the FCC directed to write rules keeping the tier's rates reasonable — giving households a low-cost option instead of forcing them to buy large bundles.

Extends the 'program access' rules to all multichannel video programming and bans new exclusive distribution contracts (existing ones must end within 120 days), so satellite and other competing distributors could obtain popular programming that cable-affiliated vendors had locked up.

Lets local franchising authorities keep FCC rate regulation in place — after a public hearing — where the cable operator is not providing an 'acceptable range of programming choices,' and gives subscribers and other residents the right to appear and present evidence at that hearing.

analysis.who_pays: Cable operators would lose the ability to set unregulated rates only for the new bare-bones tier and would have to unbundle it; cable-affiliated programming companies would lose exclusive distribution contracts and could no longer refuse or discriminate against non-cable distributors. Subscribers on expanded cable packages bore the risk: outside communities where a local authority certified a failure of programming choice, FCC rate regulation of those tiers would end after March 31, 1999, leaving rates to the market.
analysis.who_pays_short: Cable-affiliated programmers; expanded-tier subscribers facing deregulated rates

drawbacks.text: The bill sunsets FCC rate regulation of cable programming service tiers after March 31, 1999 unless a local franchising authority affirmatively goes through a hearing process and certifies a failure of programming choice — meaning in most communities rates for expanded tiers would simply be deregulated, and cable rates had risen sharply after earlier deregulation in the 1996 telecommunications law.

The local certification standard is narrow and weak: it looks only at whether subscribers get an 'acceptable range of programming choices,' not whether prices are fair; the certification lasts only one year, and the FCC can rescind it if it finds the local determination 'arbitrary and capricious' at the cable operator's request.

The lifeline tier is bare-bones — only local broadcast and required access channels — and operators are forbidden from adding anything to it, so it is a minimal fallback rather than an affordable full service, and it does nothing for the majority of viewing (cable news, sports, entertainment) that drives bills up.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a genuine bargain: it trades away rate regulation of most cable packages — a real risk to monthly bills, with the burden on local governments to prove each operator deserves continued regulation — in exchange for concrete consumer gains (a price-regulated basic tier, an end to exclusive programming contracts, and hearing rights for subscribers) and a real boost to satellite competition. Whether the trade favored consumers depended on whether competition from satellite would actually restrain cable rates, which the bill simply gambled on.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to a House Commerce subcommittee in August 1998 and never brought up for any vote before the Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Rep. Billy Tauzin (R-LA) introduced the bill on July 29, 1998 with Rep. Edward Markey (D-MA) as the co-lead, and it was referred to the House Commerce Committee the same day.
On August 17, 1998 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Telecommunications, Trade, and Consumer Protection, and no further action was ever taken on it.
The Congress ended on January 3, 1999, and the bill expired in subcommittee with 4 cosponsors (3 Democrats, 1 Republican) and no vote of any kind in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Cable operators and cable-affiliated programming companies were better off because the bill died: FCC rate regulation of cable tiers stayed on the books and exclusive distribution contracts continued, while the satellite competition and cheap lifeline-tier provisions that might have pressured the industry never became law.

for.name: Rep. W.J. (Billy) Tauzin
for.role: House sponsor; chairman of the Commerce Subcommittee on Telecommunications, Trade, and Consumer Protection, which received the bill
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gathered 4 cosponsors

for.name: Rep. Edward Markey
for.role: Co-lead original cosponsor; senior Democrat on the telecommunications subcommittee
for.what_they_did: Joined Tauzin in introducing the bill as an original cosponsor

sides.party_line_note: A Republican chairman and a senior Democrat introduced the bill together and its 4 cosponsors split 3-1 between the parties, but no vote was ever held, so opposition was never measured on the record.

industries.note: The bill's centerpiece would end FCC rate regulation of cable programming service tiers after March 31, 1999 unless a local authority certifies otherwise — freeing operators to set market rates on most of what subscribers buy. The required bare-bones lifeline tier is a modest offset, and cable operators never had to give up anything because the bill died.

These companies controlled popular satellite-delivered networks through exclusive contracts. The bill would ban new exclusives, force existing ones to end within 120 days, and prohibit price discrimination against non-cable distributors — opening their programming to satellite rivals. The bill's death left their exclusive deals intact.

Extending program access rules to all multichannel video programming and ending exclusive contracts would let satellite services carry the same networks as cable and compete for subscribers head-to-head. The bill's death preserved the cable-affiliated bottleneck.

They would gain the gatekeeper power to keep rate regulation alive after a public hearing, but only under a narrow programming-choice test and only one year at a time. Subscribers would get the right to appear and present evidence at those hearings.
